summary:
Vermont is among the most protective US states on gender-identity nondiscrimination as of July 2026, though a national legal risk assessment notes that the federal layer is under attack through the DC House bathroom ban, so that tier on its own can no longer be considered fully protective.

State law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, signed May 22, 2007 by Governor Jim Douglas, and took effect July 1, 2007.

Vermont's hate crime law provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's gender identity; gender identity was added in 1999 to the 1990 law that originally covered sexual orientation. The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott, effective July 1, 2021.

The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying, cyberbullying and harassment based on gender identity in all educational institutions. In October 2023 the Vermont Department of Education unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms.

Since July 1, 2018 all single-user public bathrooms in Vermont must be marked as gender-neutral under a bill signed in May 2018.

Vermont permits both preoperative and post-operative transgender people to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other state-issued documents upon court order supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner. Effective July 1, 2022, individuals born in Vermont can change their sex marker to male, female or X based on self-determination without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission, under a bill signed in April 2022 (H.628, Act 88, approved April 6, 2022, amending 18 V.S.A. § 5112). Since July 1, 2019 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs with no documentation needed.

Since 2013 all health insurers underwriting in Vermont are required to cover transgender care including sex reassignment surgery. In May 2023 a law effective immediately by emergency clause legally protects, defends and shields transgender and non-binary people accessing gender-affirming healthcare across state lines coming into Vermont. Vermont has shield laws enacted in 2023 and 2024 that are enforceable against out-of-state action.

Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors, which includes transgender minors, was banned by S.132 (Act 138), signed May 25, 2016 and effective July 1, 2016, treating its performance on minors as unprofessional conduct under 18 V.S.A. §§ 8351-8353 and related 26 V.S.A. licensing statutes.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Vermont since September 1, 2009, the first state to adopt it via legislature and governor rather than court decision; civil unions for same-sex couples were introduced in July 2000 following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court equal marriage benefits ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has full state-level recognition.

In 2023 Mid Vermont Christian School's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl, citing fairness and safety, and was as a result forbidden from competition by the Vermont Principals' Association.
tangentialFactors:
Vermont's protective posture sits within a national landscape where the federal layer is under active challenge; a July 2026 national legal risk assessment notes the DC House bathroom ban as evidence that the protective tier alone can no longer be treated as fully protective.

Compared with states that have enacted bathroom bans, care bans or document restrictions, Vermont moves in the opposite direction on every one of these axes: gender-neutral single-user bathrooms since 2018, self-determined birth-certificate markers since 2022, X on licences since 2019, and insurance coverage of transgender care since 2013.

Vermont's shield laws are enforceable against out-of-state action, placing it among a smaller group of states with such protections, which matters for a visitor crossing state lines within New England.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the full stack of Vermont protections: nondiscrimination coverage across employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices; hate-crime penalties keyed to gender identity; anti-bullying protections in all educational institutions; and the 2023 Department of Education policy defending transgender and non-binary students in schools.

Birth certificates can be amended to male, female or X on self-determination without court order or medical permission since July 1, 2022, and driver's licences and state IDs have offered X with no documentation since July 1, 2019.

Conversion therapy on LGBT minors has been prohibited since July 1, 2016 as unprofessional conduct subject to licensing discipline. The gay and/or trans panic defence has been unavailable since July 1, 2021.

Health insurers underwriting in Vermont have been required to cover transgender care, including sex reassignment surgery, since 2013, and the 2023 shield law protects residents obtaining gender-affirming healthcare across state lines.

Adoption is open to single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent irrespective of marital status, following a June 1993 Vermont Supreme Court ruling in favour of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons.
outOfScopeNotes:
The July 2026 risk assessment's caveat that the federal layer is under attack through the DC House bathroom ban is stated at the national level; how any specific federal measure applies to a visitor in Vermont at the time of travel is not resolved in these sources and should be checked against the current operative position.

Whether Vermont's shield laws would be tested against a specific out-of-state prosecution or extradition request is not documented in the inventory.

The inventory does not address Vermont-specific airport screening practice, in-state detention conditions for trans people, or state-level enforcement data on the hate-crime and nondiscrimination provisions.
